statement: Susan Kellogg, Law and the Transformation of Aztec Culture, 1500-1700 (University of Oklahoma Press, 1995), based on 73 property lawsuits before the Real Audiencia (1536-1700) plus pre-contact-era wills, documents that pre-Hispanic Mexica women held real property and inheritance rights — inheritance passed through both male and female lines, and women could and did will property, including favoring female heirs in some surviving wills. Kellogg's central finding is directional: colonial Spanish law subsequently ERODED these rights, shifting Mexica households from bilateral/multifamily kinship structures toward Spanish-style nuclear patrilineal families and increasing women's legal subordination over the 16th-17th centuries — i.e. the pre-conquest baseline was less patriarchal in property terms than the colonial trajectory that followed it.

sources.citation: Kellogg, Susan. Law and the Transformation of Aztec Culture, 1500-1700. Norman: University of Oklahoma Press, 1995.
sources.author: Susan Kellogg

does_not_demonstrate: That Mexica women's legal status was static across the 1500-1700 period, as opposed to a documented trajectory of erosion under colonial Spanish law relative to a real pre-conquest baseline
